title: How We Got the New Testament
subtitle: The criteria, the Muratorian fragment, Athanasius in 367, and what Nicaea never decided.
triageNote: The twenty-seven books themselves are not in dispute among Christians; Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Bibles carry the same New Testament, which is a fact worth pausing over. What divides the traditions, and the scholars, is the account of how those books came to be the list, and what kind of authority did the deciding. That question shapes whole theologies of church and Scripture, and it deserves better than the legends told about it, including the durable myth that a council at Nicaea voted books in and out. Nothing of the sort happened, and the true story is better than the legend.
question: Within a generation of the crucifixion, Christian communities possessed letters of Paul, and within two generations, written Gospels. By the late second century, lists were being drawn. In 367, bishop Athanasius of Alexandria circulated an Easter letter naming exactly our twenty-seven books, the first surviving document to do so, and councils at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 affirmed the same list. The historical sequence is reasonably clear. The question underneath it is not. When the early church sorted Matthew from the Gospel of Thomas, was it conferring authority or recognizing it. Did the books become canon when the church listed them, or were they canon from the day they were written, with the lists merely catching up. And what do the slow cases, Hebrews doubted in the West, Revelation doubted in the East, 2 Peter doubted nearly everywhere for a time, tell us about how God gives a Bible to a church.
whyItMatters:
In 2003 a novel informed many millions of readers that the Bible as we have it was collated by the pagan emperor Constantine, that he commissioned a new Bible omitting the gospels that spoke of Christ's human traits, and that the matter was settled by a vote at the Council of Nicaea in 325. Almost every reader of this page has met someone who believes a version of that. Here is what the council of 325 actually addressed: the deity of Christ against Arius, the date of Easter, and church order. No surviving record of Nicaea, and the records are substantial, mentions the canon at all. The legend of books placed under a table and miraculously sorted appears in an anonymous Greek note centuries later, and the Constantine story as popularly told is fiction. But the fiction works on people because the true story is unknown to them, and an unknown true story always loses to a vivid false one.

So learn the true one, because it carries weight either way. If the canon emerged the way one side says, by the church's gradual, prayerful recognition of books that bore apostolic authority from birth, then your New Testament rests on something older and stronger than any committee. If it emerged the way another side says, by the authoritative judgment of a church Christ empowered to judge, then the church that gave you the list has claims on you that Protestants have not fully reckoned with. And if it emerged the way the critics say, as the winning party's library, then the question of why these books and not others is the question of whether Christianity is true. The stakes are not antiquarian. The table of contents is a theology, and you inherited it. This page is about whether you can give an account of it.

positions.name: The self-attesting canon
positions.inOneLine: The books were canon from the moment of writing because of what they are, apostolic witness bearing divine qualities, and the church did not create the list but recognized, over time, what God had given.
positions.bestCase:
Begin with a distinction that untangles most of this debate: the difference between canon and canon list. The list, the official census, comes late, Athanasius in 367, the councils after him. The canon, the existence of authoritative apostolic writings binding on the churches, is as old as the writings themselves. When Peter, in the sixties of the first century, classes Paul's letters with the other Scriptures, the canon is already functioning. When Paul tells the Colossians to have his letter read also in Laodicea, and tells the Thessalonians that his letter is to be read to all the brothers, he is issuing covenant documents to communities, with authority, on purpose. The church did not wait three hundred years for a Bible. She was born holding one testament and watched the other being written.

Michael Kruger has given this view its fullest modern form, and his account stands on three legs that support each other. First, divine qualities: the books carry the marks of their Author, the same beauty and power and harmony with the rest of God's word that has always distinguished Scripture, and the Spirit enables Christ's people to perceive them, my sheep hear my voice. Second, apostolic origins: the canon is the deposit of the apostles, the men Christ authorized as his witnesses, which is why apostolicity, not popularity, was the early church's first question about any book, written by an apostle or the close companion of one, within the apostolic age. Third, corporate reception: the church's slow, broad, unforced convergence on these books is itself evidence, the predictable result of the Spirit working in the community, not the cause of the books' authority but the effect of it.

Now test the theory against the actual history, because it fits like a key. Nobody convened to choose the four Gospels. By the time Irenaeus writes around 180, the fourfold Gospel is so settled he compares it to the four winds and four corners of the earth, settled across communities scattered from Gaul to Egypt with no mechanism to coordinate. The Muratorian fragment, our earliest surviving list, usually dated to Rome around 170 to 200, already has the spine of the New Testament, four Gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, and more. What the church did debate, honestly and slowly, were the margins, Hebrews because the West doubted its authorship, 2 Peter because its Greek differs from 1 Peter, Revelation because the East grew wary after the Montanist excesses. And notice what those debates were about: apostolicity. The church was not asking which books do we prefer. She was asking which books are from the apostles, which is to say, she was submitting to a standard outside herself, the posture of recognition, not of sovereignty. Athanasius's own verb in 367 gives the whole game away. He does not say these books are hereby decreed. He says these are the books handed down and confirmed as divine, and he is at pains to add, in these alone the teaching of godliness is proclaimed, let no one add to them or take from them. A man does not talk that way about a list he thinks his office created.

positions.name: The church-authority view
positions.inOneLine: The canon is known with certainty only because the church, teaching with Christ's own authority, discerned and defined it, so the Bible and the church that canonized it cannot be played against each other.
positions.bestCase:
Let me put the difficulty to you as plainly as Augustine put it sixteen centuries ago, writing against the Manichees around 397: I would not believe the gospel itself, he said, unless the authority of the catholic church moved me. That sentence scandalizes my Protestant friends, but stay with it, because it describes their situation as much as mine. Here is a simple, awkward fact. Scripture nowhere contains its own table of contents. No verse tells you there are twenty-seven New Testament books, or that Hebrews is in and the Shepherd of Hermas, beloved and read in the churches for generations, is out. The inspired books do not arrive with inspired labels. So the knowledge of which books are inspired, the very knowledge on which sola scriptura depends, is itself a piece of knowledge that comes from somewhere other than Scripture. It comes from the church. Every Christian who opens a Bible is trusting the church's discernment before he reads a word, and my position simply says out loud what everyone is doing.

And consider how the discernment actually worked, because the history is on my side of the ledger. The criteria the early church applied, apostolic origin, agreement with the rule of faith, universal use in the churches, are all ecclesial criteria, judgments only a living, teaching community could make. Who knew which books came from apostolic men. The churches that received them, Rome for Mark, Asia for John, the communities whose memory was the evidence. Who possessed the rule of faith against which a book's teaching was measured. The church, who had carried the gospel orally before a line of the New Testament existed, for the faith was preached before it was written, and the writings were tested against the preaching, not the other way around. When the hard cases came, who settled them. Not private judgment, which gave the church Marcion, who in about 140 cut the canon down to one mutilated Gospel and ten letters of Paul, and would have starved the church of her Scriptures. The bishops settled them, in synods, at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397, lists later confirmed at Florence in 1442 and defined at Trent in 1546. The canon of Scripture is, historically and irreversibly, an act of the church's teaching office.

Do not mistake this for placing the church above God's word. The First Vatican Council said precisely the opposite: the church holds these books as sacred not because she later approved them by her authority, but because, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they have God as their author, and were as such committed to the church. The books' authority is from God. The certain knowledge of which books, that is the gift Christ gave through the church, the pillar and buttress of the truth, the household to which the Scriptures were entrusted. My Protestant brother believes in a self-collecting Bible and cannot name the mechanism. I can name it. Christ promised the Spirit would guide his church into all truth, and the canon in your hands is what that guidance looks like when it is written down.
advocates: the Roman Catholic tradition (Trent, 1546; Vatican I, 1870)
the Eastern Orthodox tradition, with its own accents

positions.name: The historical-development view
positions.inOneLine: The canon is the contingent outcome of second- through fourth-century church history, the library of the party that prevailed, and honest method studies how the boundary was drawn rather than assuming it was inevitable.
positions.bestCase:
I am going to ask you to do something uncomfortable but clarifying: study the canon the way you would study any other historical artifact, with the providence question bracketed, not denied, just bracketed, so the evidence can speak in its own order. Do that, and a story emerges with real dates and real causes, and it is not the story of a list quietly recognizing itself.

The earliest church had no New Testament. It had the Jewish Scriptures, oral tradition, and living prophecy. The first person we know to have promulgated a defined collection of Christian Scripture was Marcion, around 140, and whether he provoked the church's canon or merely accelerated it, the fact stands that boundary-drawing began in controversy, as it would continue. Walter Bauer argued in 1934 that early Christianity was not a single orthodox stream with heretical eddies but a plurality of Christianities, differing by region, and that what we call orthodoxy is, in large part, the tradition of Rome and its allies, which won. Bauer overstated his case, his critics have landed real blows, but his core observation survives every rebuttal: the boundaries were contested, for a long time, by serious people. Christians in good standing read the Gospel of Peter in church at Rhossus until a bishop, Serapion, around 200, withdrew it after checking its doctrine. The Shepherd of Hermas appears in our oldest complete New Testament codex, Sinaiticus, along with the Epistle of Barnabas. Eusebius, writing around 325, still sorts the books into acknowledged, disputed, and spurious, with James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John sitting in the disputed column, and Revelation listed, remarkably, in two columns at once. That is the canon's actual state of play three centuries in: a firm core, yes, I grant the core gladly, and a margin still moving.

And what moved the margin was history, not magic. The criteria themselves, apostolicity, orthodoxy, catholicity, are circular in a way the pious account never faces: a book was apostolic if it agreed with the church's teaching, and the church's teaching was apostolic because it agreed with the books. Decisions tracked the needs of an institution consolidating itself against Gnostics, Montanists, and Marcionites, and the final ratifications, Athanasius's letter of 367, the North African councils of the 390s, belong to the age when the church had imperial standing and needed uniform texts. None of this requires cynicism. The selectors were sincere, and, I will say it plainly, they mostly chose the oldest and best books on the table; the canonical Gospels are earlier and historically richer than the apocryphal ones, and the church knew it. But sincerity does not make an outcome necessary, and the believer who claims the canon could not have been otherwise is claiming to know history's counterfactuals. The honest position is humbler: these books were canonized because these communities, in these conflicts, with these criteria, prevailed. Whether God superintended that process is a faith judgment. I only insist that you make it as a judgment, with the evidence in view, and not as an assumption you were never shown.
advocates: Walter Bauer (Orthodoxy and Heresy in Earliest Christianity, 1934)
keyTexts: Revelation 22:18-19 (a book guarding its own border)
1 Corinthians 14:29 (testing the spirits as ongoing practice)

biblicalEvidence.summary: Peter refers to all of Paul's letters, notes that the ignorant twist them as they do the other Scriptures, and thereby classes apostolic letters with Scripture inside the New Testament period itself. Canon-consciousness on the page, in the first century.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the historical-development view, which must either accept first-century canon-consciousness or date 2 Peter late, and many of its scholars do argue the letter is second-century, which is itself a reminder that the evidence and the frameworks travel together.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The development view replies that even on a late date the verse only proves Paul's letters were being collected and revered, not that a bounded canon existed. The church-authority view notes the verse assumes a community that knows which letters are Paul's and how Scripture is rightly read, the church doing exactly the work this view describes.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul writes, the Scripture says, and then quotes two sentences: one from Deuteronomy 25:4, and one, the laborer deserves his wages, found in Luke 10:7. If the second citation is from Luke, a Gospel is being called Scripture within the apostolic generation.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that dates all canon-consciousness to the second century or later.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The development view answers that the saying of Jesus circulated orally and in early collections, so Paul may quote the saying, not the book of Luke, and the church-authority view agrees that is possible while observing that either way, the words of Jesus carried scriptural force in the churches before any list existed, authority running ahead of paperwork, which all three views can absorb.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The self-attesting canon, with church-authority claiming the second verse
biblicalEvidence.summary: My sheep hear my voice. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth. Together, the texts behind both recognition theology, the flock knows the Shepherd's voice in the true books, and guidance theology, the Spirit leads the church to truth she did not yet possess.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the development view if taken as promise, since it grounds an expectation that the sorting process was not left to sociology, though the development view rightly notes the verses name no books.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The self-attesting view reads John 10 as the mechanism of canon: Christ's people, corporately and over time, recognize Christ's voice in apostolic writing. The church-authority view reads John 16 as addressed to the apostles and their successors, the teaching office guided into truth, canon included. The development view observes that both readings are theology laid over the history, and that men quoting these very verses disagreed for centuries about Hebrews and Revelation.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, with a sharp edge for everyone
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul directs that his letter be read in Laodicea, and that you also read the letter from Laodicea. Apostolic letters circulated by command, publicly read like Scripture, from the start. And the Laodicean letter is lost.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for everyone, honestly. A letter Paul commanded to be read did not survive into anyone's canon, which presses the self-attesting view, did an inspired writing perish, presses the church-authority view, did the church misplace an apostolic document, and gives the development view its favorite kind of evidence, contingency.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The self-attesting view answers that inspiration attaches to what God intended for the church's permanent canon, and providence preserved exactly that, apostolic does not automatically mean canonical, Paul wrote other letters too, as 1 Corinthians 5:9 shows. The church-authority view says the church received what was given for the whole church, and the development view says the survival of texts tracked the usefulness of texts, which is how libraries work.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The historical-development view, used carefully by all
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul warns the church not to be shaken by a spirit or a spoken word or a letter seeming to be from us. Forgery in apostolic names is already a live danger in the fifties of the first century, which is why Paul signs with his own hand.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any romantic picture in which the early church faced no counterfeits and needed no criteria. Verifying letters was a problem from the beginning because deception was a practice from the beginning.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The development view takes the verse as its charter: where forgery exists, sorting exists, and sorting is a human, criterial, fallible process. The self-attesting view draws the opposite moral from the same verse: the apostles themselves taught the churches to test what claimed their names, so the church's later sifting of books was obedience to apostolic instruction, not improvisation. The church-authority view adds that the test Paul gives, the tradition you were taught by us, is the rule of faith functioning exactly as Catholic theology describes.

biblicalEvidence.summary: I warn everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues described in this book. Popularly cited as God sealing the whole Bible, since Revelation stands last.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the popular argument, because the warning belongs to the book of Revelation about itself, echoing Deuteronomy 4:2, and was written before any bound Bible existed and long before Revelation stood last in one.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All three views actually agree here, which makes the verse useful: it shows a biblical author claiming complete, untouchable authority for a prophetic writing at the moment of writing, which the self-attesting view generalizes, the church-authority view says required ecclesial confirmation, Revelation being among the longest-doubted books in the East, and the development view cites as evidence that border-guarding language was a genre convention of the age.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The historical-development view, embraced by the self-attesting view
biblicalEvidence.summary: Many have undertaken to compile a narrative, Luke says, and he writes his own orderly account from eyewitness tradition so that Theophilus may have certainty. The New Testament's own preface admits a plurality of early Christian writings, sorted by quality and testimony.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any account that imagines the canonical four falling from heaven with no literary environment around them.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The development view reads it as the situation it describes everywhere, many texts, human evaluation. The self-attesting view replies that Luke's preface is precisely the difference: eyewitness chain, careful method, the apostolic deposit, which is why the church kept Luke and let the many fade, the criteria were real and the canonical books really met them. The church-authority view notes that certainty, Luke's stated goal, is delivered to Theophilus through an authorized teacher, catechesis inside the community, the things you have been taught.

weighing:
My judgment, held tentatively and stated plainly.

The development scholars have taught me things I will not unlearn: the margins really were debated for centuries, Eusebius's disputed column is real, Sinaiticus really does bind Hermas after Revelation, and a faith that needs to hide any of that is weaker than the faith I hold. But when I stand back from the data they have so carefully assembled, what astonishes me is not the contingency, it is the convergence. Communities scattered from Lyon to Alexandria, with no mechanism of coordination, no imperial sponsor for the first three centuries, and every incentive to multiply texts, converged on the same four Gospels by the mid-second century and the same core of Paul earlier still. The books that were debated were debated about one question, apostolicity, which means the church was measuring herself against a standard she did not invent and could not move. That looks like recognition, not manufacture. The sheep were listening for a voice.

So I find the self-attesting account the most truthful to the evidence as well as to the theology, and I want to say why without triumphalism. Its strength is that it predicts exactly the history we find: instant, unforced authority for the books at the center, because the voice was unmistakable, and slow, careful, criteria-driven sorting at the edges, because the church was being honest rather than hasty. Three centuries of patience with 2 Peter is not a scandal. It is what taking the question seriously looks like.

And yet I will not pretend the church-authority men leave me unmoved. Augustine's sentence has a hook in it. Somebody did hand me this list, and the Protestant who acts as if his table of contents floated to him directly from heaven is not more spiritual than the Catholic, only more forgetful. My answer, the one I actually rest in, is that the Spirit's witness and the church's reception are not rivals but the same event described from two sides, God's voice and God's people hearing it. The canon closed the way a door closes when the last family member is home. Nobody voted. Everyone knew.
charitableDisagreement:
What is each side guarding. The self-attesting view guards the principle that God's word does not derive its authority from human institutions, which is the whole Reformation in one sentence. The church-authority view guards the visible community without which no one alive would possess a Bible at all, and asks Protestants a question they should feel the weight of rather than wave away. The development view guards the historical record itself, and the church owes its critical historians more gratitude than it usually pays, because the legends they demolished, Nicaea voting on books among them, were doing the faith real damage in the mouths of its defenders.

Is this a hill to die on. The contents of the New Testament canon, remarkably, divide no one here, Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant read the same twenty-seven books, and that shared shelf is one of the quiet miracles of church history. The theory of the canon, recognition or ratification or contingency, is a real and consequential disagreement, but it is an argument among people holding identical Bibles, which ought to set its temperature. Learn the dates, Marcion around 140, the Muratorian fragment within a generation or two of him, Irenaeus by 180, Eusebius around 325, Athanasius in 367, Hippo and Carthage in the 390s. Learn them well enough to correct the legends gently, including the legends your own side prefers. The canon has been carried to you across twenty centuries by hands from every one of these traditions. The least you owe the carriers is the true story.

relatedDebates.topic: How we got the Old Testament
relatedDebates.note: The earlier half of the same question, with the same principles in play, recognition against conferral, usage against decree, and an older, thinner evidence trail. The two pages are designed to be read together, and the traditions answer both with the same instincts.

Canon asks which books; textual criticism asks whether we have what those books originally said. The skeptical argument usually runs the two together, and taking them apart is half the answer. The manuscripts page in this set takes up the second question with the variants honestly counted.

Thomas, Peter, Philip, Judas, and the rest, mostly second- and third-century, mostly Gnostic in flavor, none of them eyewitness-rooted biography of the canonical kind. Reading even a few pages of them is the fastest cure for the suspicion that the church suppressed equally good rivals, which is why every position on this page recommends exactly that.
